extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, literary critics, and readers interested in standards for "moral fiction"
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for producing or evaluating fiction that is morally serious — fiction that aspires to help readers live more fully by presenting truthful, proportioned, and artful accounts of human life and value. The guidance addresses both ethical aims and literary craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral seriousness (central ethical purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work must be made with moral seriousness — a deliberate, sustained concern with human good and how people should live, not mere cleverness, irony, or aesthetic posturing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gardner argues moral seriousness is not preaching; it means the artist cares about right and wrong and intends the work to illuminate moral reality. Anti-patterns: works that are amoral, gratuitously cynical, or treat moral issues only as intellectual puzzles without human sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and honesty to experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction must tell the truth as the author sees it about human beings and their moral situations; it should not falsify or sentimentalize reality for ideological or fashionable effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth involves accurate particulars, credible motives, plausible consequences. Avoid sentimental simplification, facile moralizing, or deliberate perversity that twists character or event merely to shock or demonstrate a theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion and respect for human worth
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should manifest sympathy and respect for the complexity and dignity of human life even when depicting vice, error, or degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compassion does not mean excusing wrongdoing; it means representing characters with sufficient depth that their suffering and choices matter. Anti-patterns: contemptuous portrayal of people, treating characters as mere examples to be ridiculed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious intellectual and emotional engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The work must engage both intellect and imagination — thoughtfulness about consequences, motives, and moral questions combined with emotional intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good moral fiction stimulates reflection and feeling; it resists detached irony or clinical cleverness that prevents readers from caring. Avoid cool cleverness that masks emptiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral complexity and nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction should present moral problems with nuance, allowing for ambiguity and struggle rather than offering glib answers or one-dimensional villains/heroes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative should permit readers to weigh competing values and witness characters' moral growth or failure. Anti-patterns: simplistic didactic tales, facile moral allegories that flatten experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and moral causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions in the story should carry believable moral consequences; good and evil should have consequences that feel earned and intelligible within the world of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This excludes arbitrary impunity for evil or false rewards for vice; it also cautions against contrived punishments that serve only to moralize. The causal chain must be credible to preserve moral teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of didacticism and sermonizing
rubrics_metrics.description: While the work is morally serious, it must not preach or lecture; moral insight should emerge organically from character, plot, and scene rather than from explicit authorial instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show, don't tell: let moral meaning arise from dramatic situation and precise detail. Anti-patterns: authorial intrusions, forced speeches, and parable-like characters whose only function is to embody a thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic excellence and craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral intent is not enough; the fiction must be artistically good — controlled language, credible characterization, disciplined structure, and energetic plotting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gardner stresses that moral fiction should meet high standards of form and craft. Technical failure will undermine moral aims. Examples of craft: precise detail, vivid scene construction, well-shaped narrative arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of form and moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral vision of the work must be embodied in its formal choices — point of view, narrative structure, tone, and style — so that form and ethical content reinforce one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid formal gimmicks or deliberately fragmented techniques that sabotage coherence of meaning. Use stylistic means that allow moral perception to arise naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and seriousness of the artist
rubrics_metrics.description: The author must be sincerely committed to the moral stakes of the work; irony, posturing, or fashionable detachment that masks lack of conviction weakens the fiction's moral force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity shows not as piety but as disciplined attention and honest uncertainty. Anti-patterns: ironic nihilism presented as profundity, cynical stance adopted for aesthetic currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for complexity of human motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' motives must be depicted as multifaceted and internally coherent rather than as mere functions of plot or symbolic devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide particularizing detail that explains behavior; avoid thin types and allegorical simplifications. Moral insight grows from understanding motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of sensationalism and gratuitous cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Depicting suffering or evil should seek moral illumination rather than merely exploiting shock value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphic or shocking elements must serve a larger moral or artistic purpose; gratuitous brutality that numbs sympathy or serves only to amaze is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to enlarge readers' moral imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should help readers imagine alternative ways of living, empathize with others, and see the moral dimension of ordinary life more clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective moral fiction deepens compassion and expands understanding rather than simply confirming readers' prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of moral perception without simple prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should offer clear perception about value and worth while resisting formulaic prescriptions for conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity means honest apprehension of right and wrong; it does not mean issuing rules. Let scenes illuminate rather than prescribe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral seriousness must be courageous and unpopular if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral fiction may need to oppose prevailing fashions and take risks to speak truthfully about human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gardner defends writers who risk unpopularity by insisting on ethical seriousness rather than colluding with despair or fashionable amoral postures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of false pieties and sentimental religiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute shallow piety or mawkish sentiment for real moral insight; spiritual language must be grounded in truthful depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antidote: concrete detail, honest failure, and humility rather than easy consolations or moral smokescreens.
